subject: food-technology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: The Fairtrade mark on a product mainly indicates that:
options: Producers in developing countries received a fair price and conditions
The food is low in fat
questions.explain: Fairtrade guarantees producers in developing countries a fair price and better working conditions.

questions.q: Turning wheat into flour is an example of:
questions.explain: Primary processing converts a raw food, such as wheat into flour or milk into cream, into a usable form.

questions.q: Food that is 'reared' refers to food that is:
questions.explain: Reared food comes from farmed animals raised for meat, eggs or dairy, such as cattle, pigs and poultry.

options: Given access to outdoor space to roam
questions.explain: Free-range hens have access to the outdoors during the day rather than being kept only in cages or barns.

questions.q: A 'carbon footprint' of a food refers to:
options: The total greenhouse gases produced across its life cycle
questions.explain: A carbon footprint is the total greenhouse gas emissions from producing, transporting and using a food.

questions.q: Fish that is 'caught' is an example of food that is:
questions.explain: Wild fish is caught from the sea or rivers, as opposed to farmed fish which is reared.

questions.q: Intensive farming is mainly characterised by:
options: Low yields and high welfare space
High output from limited land or space, often at lower cost
questions.explain: Intensive farming aims to maximise output from limited land or space, often keeping costs low.

questions.q: Which farming method avoids artificial pesticides and fertilisers and follows strict welfare standards?
questions.explain: Organic farming avoids artificial chemicals and follows strict animal welfare and environmental standards.

questions.q: Which of these is the best way for a household to reduce food waste?
options: Planning meals, storing food correctly and using leftovers
Cooking far more than is needed
Buying in bulk and throwing away leftovers
questions.explain: Planning meals, correct storage and using leftovers help cut food waste at home.

options: People having reliable access to enough safe, affordable food
questions.explain: Food security means people always have reliable access to enough safe and nutritious food.

questions.q: Turning flour into bread or cakes is an example of:
questions.explain: Secondary processing turns primary-processed foods, such as flour, into other products like bread and pasta.

options: The number of calories in food
The distance food travels from where it is produced to where it is eaten
questions.explain: Food miles measure the distance food travels from production to the consumer, linked to carbon emissions.
